title: The middle class and vulnerability to income poverty: Implications for social protection in the Philippines
authors: Cabalfin, D. L. D.; Albert, J. R. G.; Mahmoud, M. A.
tldr: Using FIES-LFS data from 2018, 2021, and 2023, this Philippine study finds vulnerability to income poverty affects 30.0% of households—2.75 times the official poverty rate—with 86% of the vulnerable experiencing income volatility, implying social protection must expand beyond poverty relief to proactive resilience building for the low-income and lower middle-income classes.
problem_and_motivation: The Philippines aspires to become a predominantly middle-class society by 2040, but traditional poverty measures underestimate the at-risk population. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of recent poverty reduction gains and the vulnerability of many households—including middle-income—to economic shocks. Static poverty head counts do not capture forward-looking risk of falling into poverty, which is crucial for designing effective social protection. There was a need to measure vulnerability using Philippine household data, decompose its sources, and derive policy implications for social protection as the country transitions toward upper-middle-income status.
approach: Employed the Chaudhuri and Datt (2001) methodology to estimate household vulnerability to income poverty as the probability of being income-poor in the next period.
Used merged Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES) and Labor Force Survey (LFS) microdata from the Philippine Statistics Authority for 2018, 2021, and 2023.
Estimated per capita household income as a function of observable household and community characteristics using three-step feasible generalized least squares (FGLS).
Supplemented household models with infrastructure indices from the 2020 Census of Population and Housing and rainfall shock data from PAGASA weather stations.
Decomposed vulnerability into two sources: high-volatility income vulnerable (fluctuating income above poverty line) and low-mean-income vulnerable (persistently low income below poverty line).
Compared vulnerability estimates across urban-rural areas, regions, education levels, employment sectors, and income classes for 2018, 2021, and 2023.
findings: Vulnerability to income poverty affects 30.0% of Filipino households in 2023, which is 2.75 times the household poverty incidence of 10.9%—demonstrating that traditional poverty measures significantly underestimate the at-risk population.

86% of vulnerable households experience high income volatility, while 73% of the highly vulnerable have persistently low incomes—households are vulnerable for distinctly different reasons requiring differentiated interventions.
Rural vulnerability is 43.0% compared to 20.0% in urban areas, with stark regional variation from 9.0% in NCR to 76.0% in rural BARMM.
The vulnerability-to-poverty ratio increased from 2.40 in 2018 to 2.75 in 2023, meaning the gap between actual poverty and future poverty risk is widening.
44% of low-income but non-poor households and 11% of lower middle-income households face significant vulnerability—suggesting middle-class gains remain fragile.
Agriculture is the highest-risk sector with 60.0% vulnerability rate and 25.0% poverty rate, while services has only 19.0% vulnerability and 6.0% poverty.

Education is a key protective factor: households headed by tertiary-educated individuals have only 5.0% vulnerability and 2.0% poverty, compared to 75% vulnerability for those with less than primary education.
Provinces with low communications infrastructure have 68% vulnerability versus 29% in high-infrastructure provinces—infrastructure is a critical protective factor.

Only 34.9% of the Philippine population is covered by social protection, far below upper-middle-income country standards of 71.2%, and trailing Thailand (70.1%), Indonesia (54.3%), and Vietnam (38.3%).
84% of the poor are vulnerable, and 23% of the non-poor are vulnerable—many households that are currently non-poor face significant risk of falling into poverty.

key_equations.explanation: Per capita household income model where y_h is per capita income, X_h is a vector of observable household and community characteristics, β is parameters, and e_h is idiosyncratic disturbance.
Variance of the disturbance term modeled as a function of observable household and community characteristics.
Expected log income estimated from the income model parameters.
Variance of log income estimated from the variance model.

key_equations.equation: v̂_h = Φ((ln z - X_h β̂) / (X_h θ̂))
key_equations.explanation: Vulnerability estimate as the probability that household h falls below the poverty line z, using the cumulative standard normal distribution function Φ.

definitions.definition: The probability that a household will fall below the poverty line in the next period, a forward-looking measure of poverty risk distinct from observed poverty.
The variability or uncertainty of household income streams over time, identified as the primary source of vulnerability for 86% of vulnerable Filipino households.
Households whose estimated mean income falls below the poverty line and whose probability of being poor exceeds 50%, representing persistently poor households.
Households with estimated mean income above the poverty line but high income variance, making them vulnerable to falling into poverty from income shocks.
Persistent poverty resulting from low endowments, skills, or structural disadvantages, addressed through long-term human capital investments.
Temporary poverty resulting from income shocks or volatility, addressable through insurance, savings, and income stabilization mechanisms.
Philippine households with per capita income between two and twelve times the official poverty line, comprising 51.3% of households in 2023.
The percentage change in poverty headcount relative to the percentage change in GDP per capita, measuring how effectively growth translates into poverty reduction.
The Philippines' flagship conditional cash transfer program providing cash to poorest households conditional on children's school attendance and health check-ups.
The mean income shortfall of the entire population relative to the poverty line, representing the minimum cost of eliminating poverty.

citations.author: Dercon
citations.claim: Defined vulnerability as the probability of significant welfare losses due to uncertain events and provided a framework emphasizing household assets, incomes, and capabilities as protective factors.

citations.author: Albert et al.

citations.claim: Formalized the distinction between chronic/structural poverty and vulnerable/stochastic poverty, where consumption varies over time due to income shocks and limited insurance.

topics.name: Budgeting Strategies and Frameworks
topics.justification: The paper provides comprehensive data on household expenditure patterns, savings rates, and income allocation across income groups in the Philippines—fundamental information for designing budgeting frameworks. The finding that low-income households spend 72.6% on food, housing, and utilities with minimal savings (1.8% median savings rate for poor) directly informs budgeting strategies for vulnerable populations.

topics.name: Expense Tracking and Categorization Systems
topics.justification: The paper analyzes household expenditure distribution across categories (food, housing, transportation, communication, health, education, other) by income group, providing a validated categorization structure relevant to expense tracking systems. The FIES expenditure categories map directly to common budget tracking categories.

topics.name: Spending Behavior Analysis and Categorization
topics.justification: The paper documents how spending patterns differ dramatically across income groups: poor households spend 52.4% on food versus 22.3% for high-income, while education and health spending rises from 4.1% to 7.6% with income. These behavioral patterns are directly relevant to understanding spending behavior for personal finance systems.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides the most comprehensive recent empirical evidence on Filipino household income, expenditure, and vulnerability patterns, using FIES microdata from 2018-2023. It establishes that vulnerability to poverty is 2.75 times higher than measured poverty, with 86% of vulnerable households experiencing income volatility rather than persistently low income. The paper provides detailed breakdowns of household income sources, expenditure shares, savings rates, employment characteristics, and demographic profiles across income groups, regions, and urban-rural areas. For the Odin thesis, this paper provides crucial Philippine-specific context: it documents the income volatility that makes personal budgeting tools necessary, quantifies the savings gap that budgeting apps could help address, and establishes that 48.7% of Filipino households are either poor or low-income—exactly the population that would benefit from a budget management system. The paper's vulnerability framework also provides theoretical grounding for why proactive financial management tools matter.
directly_justifies: 48.7% of Filipino households are poor or low-income with minimal financial buffers, making budget management tools critical.
86% of vulnerable households experience income volatility, not just low income—budgeting tools must handle irregular income streams.
Poor households spend 52.4% of expenditures on food with only 1.8% median savings rate, indicating severe budget constraints.
Rural households face 43% vulnerability versus 20% urban, suggesting geographic targeting for budget tools.
Education is a protective factor against vulnerability—financial literacy tools align with this finding.
The Philippines has low social protection coverage (34.9%), leaving households to rely on personal financial management.
limits: The paper uses cross-sectional data rather than longitudinal household tracking, limiting causal inference about vulnerability dynamics.
The vulnerability estimates assume income is log-normally distributed and do not account for aggregate shocks or structural changes.
The paper does not address digital financial tools or mobile-based budgeting systems, which are the application domain of the Odin thesis.
The FIES survey is biennial, potentially missing rapid changes in household economic status between survey rounds.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. This is a local (Philippine) paper analyzing household income, expenditure, and vulnerability—directly relevant to personal finance management. Topic 1.A (Budgeting Strategies) is highly relevant because the paper provides comprehensive data on household expenditure patterns, savings rates, and income allocation that inform budgeting framework design. Topic 2.A (Spending Behavior Analysis) is highly relevant because the paper documents how spending behavior differs across income groups with detailed category-level breakdowns. Topic 1.B (Expense Tracking) receives medium relevance because the paper's expenditure categories map to tracking system categories but does not address tracking technology. Topics related to ML algorithms (6.A-6.B), anomaly detection (8.A-8.C), system architecture (9.A-9.C), evaluation frameworks (11.A-11.C) were scanned and rejected as the paper does not address algorithmic methods. The paper's local designation and Philippine-specific data make it directly applicable to the Odin system's target user population.

limitations: The Chaudhuri-Datt methodology uses cross-sectional data rather than panel data, which limits the ability to track actual household trajectories over time.
The model assumes idiosyncratic shocks are random and do not persist year to year, and rules out aggregate shocks or structural changes.
The vulnerability estimates use a parametric approach assuming log-normal income distribution, which may not hold for all population subgroups.
The FIES survey is conducted biennially, potentially missing rapid economic changes between survey rounds.
The paper does not account for non-income dimensions of vulnerability such as health shocks, climate events, or social exclusion.
The analysis does not address how digital financial tools or mobile-based budget management could mitigate vulnerability.
Regional and sectoral analyses are constrained by the geographic classification system used in the FIES.
remember_this: Vulnerability to poverty (30.0%) is 2.75 times higher than measured poverty (10.9%) in the Philippines—traditional poverty measures severely underestimate risk.
86% of vulnerable Filipino households experience income volatility, not persistently low income—budget tools must handle irregular income.
48.7% of Filipino households are poor or low-income with minimal savings buffers (median 1.8% savings rate for poor).
Rural vulnerability (43%) is more than double urban (20%), with BARMM rural reaching 76%.
Education is the strongest protective factor: tertiary-educated household heads have 5% vulnerability versus 75% for less than primary.
Agriculture sector has 60% vulnerability rate versus 19% in services—sectoral transition is critical.
Only 34.9% of Filipinos have social protection coverage, far below the upper-middle-income average of 71.2%.
The Philippines spends only 2.7% of GDP on social protection versus the upper-middle-income average of 8.5%.
Social protection must evolve from reactive poverty relief to proactive resilience building for the vulnerable non-poor.
Low-infrastructure provinces have dramatically higher vulnerability (68% vs 29% for high-infrastructure).
